knowledgePattern: Keep modulus signs when a trigonometric square root becomes an algebraic equation

hints.title: Preserve the square-root sign
hints.body: Use the identity 1−sin2x=cos2x, then name the cosine as a variable with its allowed range.
hints.recap: The principal square root of a square is a modulus, not automatically the original expression.
hints.pitfall: Do not assume cosine is nonnegative throughout the interval.
hints.pause: Rewrite the equation in one trigonometric variable.

recall.reminder: The principal square root of a square is a modulus, not automatically the original expression.

hints.title: Separate the modulus cases
hints.body: Solve each sign case and retain only algebraic roots compatible with that case and the cosine range.
hints.recap: Every branch must be checked against its own restrictions before converting back to angles.
hints.pitfall: A root from one sign case may violate that case.
hints.pause: Find the accepted cosine levels, then use graph symmetry to sum all their angles.

recall.reminder: Every branch must be checked against its own restrictions before converting back to angles.

solution:
1. Put c=cosx. Since 1−sin2x=|cosx|, the equation is |c|=2−2c2−c, with −1≤c≤1.

2. For c≥0, the equation gives c2+c−1=0. Only c=(5−1)/2 satisfies this case and the cosine range. It lies strictly between 0 and 1, giving angles α and 360∘−α whose sum is 360∘.

3. For c<0, the equation gives c2=1, so only c=−1 is compatible. This gives x=180∘.

4. The sum of all angles is 360∘+180∘=540∘. Neither endpoint 0 nor 360 satisfies the original equation. Answer C.
